entry.name: Bayberry & wax myrtle
entry.scientific: Morella pensylvanica and Morella cerifera; also M. caroliniensis (evergreen bayberry) in the southeastern coastal plain and M. californica (Pacific wax myrtle) on the West Coast. All four were long placed in Myrica, and USDA PLANTS, older field guides and most nursery labels still say Myrica pensylvanica, M. cerifera and M. californica — same plants. Two names in the neighbourhood are not the same plant: Morella inodora, the odorless bayberry of the northern Gulf, is a scentless member of this genus and seasons nothing, and Myrica gale (sweet gale) is a separate genus that is aromatic but NOT interchangeable — see lookalikes for both.
entry.habitat: Acid, low-nutrient, usually sandy ground in full sun, nearly always within reach of the coast. Bayberry is actinorhizal — it fixes its own nitrogen in root nodules with Frankia bacteria — so it colonises bare sterile sand where almost nothing else will, and a dense dark-green shrub island on an otherwise open sand flat is very often this plant. In the Northeast that means back-dune thickets and the damp swales behind the primary dune, the upland margins of salt marshes, pine barrens, pond and bog edges and abandoned sandy farm fields, in company with pitch pine, eastern red cedar, beach plum, black cherry, bearberry, greenbrier, Virginia creeper and a great deal of shrubby poison ivy; northern bayberry runs from the Maritimes south along the coast to North Carolina. A scatter of small disjunct populations sits on Great Lakes shorelines and in a few interior barrens — these are tracked as rare in some states and are not a foraging resource; leave them. Southern wax myrtle takes over from roughly southern New Jersey and the Delmarva south through Florida and west to eastern Texas, southeastern Oklahoma and central Arkansas, on fresh to slightly brackish shores, in pine flatwoods and savannas, on pocosin and bay-forest rims, wet prairies, hammocks and swamp margins — but also on dry xeric sandhills, and aggressively along roadsides, fencerows, powerline cuts and unburned old fields. Evergreen bayberry (M. caroliniensis) fills the wetter southeastern coastal plain between the two. Pacific wax myrtle holds the fog belt from Grays Harbor, Washington to southern California, on coastal bluffs, dune scrub, canyon bottoms and moist wooded slopes. Three habitat warnings bear directly on safety. First, this is one of the most planted landscape shrubs in the Southeast and on the West Coast, so a large share of the plants you can actually reach are nursery stock in clipped hedges standing shoulder to shoulder with oleander, cherry laurel, Florida anise and privet — which is to say, beside most of the things here that can hurt you. Second, where a dune swale or pond edge grades into saturated peat you have left bayberry ground and entered sweet gale, bog laurel and Labrador tea ground; those three meet bayberry along that seam throughout the Northeast, the Great Lakes and the Pacific Northwest, and two of them are aromatic. Third, the southeastern streamhead bogs, bayheads, ravine bottoms and bay-forest rims that hold Morella inodora and rim the wax myrtle pocosins are also the native ground of Illicium — an alternate, leathery, evergreen, strongly aromatic shrub that is not a Morella at all.
entry.indicator: The gray-green shrub band immediately behind the primary dune, where beach grass gives out and pitch pine and eastern red cedar begin — or, in the Southeast, the wax myrtle rim of a pond-pine pocosin or a wet longleaf flatwoods, with gallberry and titi. Because it makes its own nitrogen, it is usually the greenest thing standing on the poorest sand.
entry.parts:
The leaves, and only the leaves — used like a bay leaf: dried, simmered whole in stock, beans, braises, chowder and pickling brine, then fished out before the pot reaches the table. They are alternate along the twig, simple, leathery, 1.5–4 in long, widest above the middle and tapering to a narrow wedge at the base, dull to glossy dark green above and paler beneath. Margins vary by species, and this is where published descriptions mislead: northern bayberry is usually entire or carries a few blunt teeth on the upper third, while southern wax myrtle and Pacific wax myrtle are often distinctly serrate along much of the upper half. A toothed leaf does not rule bayberry out — which is the same as saying a toothed leaf cannot rule out hollyleaf cherry or toyon for you in California. The two constants are the RESIN DOTS, sunken golden to orange-brown glands scattered across the underside (and on both surfaces in wax myrtle), visible held to the light and gritty under a thumbnail; and the SCENT, which on a hard crush is sweet resinous balsam and candle wax — closer to bay rum than to a Mediterranean bay leaf.

THE POT IS THE DOSE, AND REMOVING THE LEAF IS NOT A SAFETY STEP. This is the most important paragraph in the entry, and it corrects the way bay-leaf substitutes are usually written up. Every deadly plant listed below poisons through the BROTH, not through the leaf you fish out. Cyanogenic glycosides (prunasin and amygdalin — cherry laurel, hollyleaf and Catalina cherry, toyon) are water-soluble and dissolve straight into the liquid; some hydrogen cyanide does boil off an open pot, but the intact glycoside stays in the stock and is cleaved to cyanide by your own gut bacteria after you drink it, and a lid keeps the free HCN in as well — 'laurel water', an infusion of exactly these leaves, was a historical murder weapon. Cardiac glycosides (oleandrin, neriine — oleander) are heat-stable and water-soluble: the documented oleander deaths are from leaf TEA and from stems used as cooking skewers, which is to say from the flavour the plant left behind after the plant itself was taken out. Grayanotoxins (the laurels, Lyonia, Leucothoe, the Labrador teas) are non-volatile, heat-stable and water-soluble — as this guide already says in its sassafras and wild blueberry entries, they are not destroyed by wilting, by shade-drying, by grinding or by the gumbo pot, and heated mad honey stays toxic. Anisatin (Illicium) is likewise extracted by hot water; every star-anise seizure case in the literature is an infusion. A 20–30 minute simmer is not a decontamination step. It is an extraction step. It is the exact procedure you would use if you were deliberately trying to move the poison out of the leaf and into the food.

SO THE RULE IS: IF A LEAF YOU CANNOT POSITIVELY IDENTIFY WENT INTO THE POT, THROW OUT THE WHOLE POT. Not the leaf — the pot. The stock, the beans, the braise, the brine, and anything already ladled out of it. Do not skim it, do not dilute it, do not taste a spoonful to see. Count the leaves into the pot and count them out again, but understand what that count is for: it is a CHOKING control, not a poison control. A missing leaf tells you to go looking; a leaf you cannot name tells you to bin the pot. If anyone has already eaten and there is any doubt at all about what went in, call Poison Control on 1-800-222-1222 immediately rather than waiting for symptoms.

WHICH MAKES IDENTIFICATION A LEAF-BY-LEAF JOB, done on the plant and again on the drying screen. Pick one leaf at a time, look at it as it comes off, and spread the picking in a single layer to check every leaf individually before it goes anywhere near a jar — once leaves are dried and mixed, the evidence of what went in is gone and every hazard here is still fully potent. Run the crush test POSITIVELY on every leaf: you confirm a bayberry by smelling the bayberry smell on that particular leaf, not by reasoning that the bush is a bayberry. And understand that the crush is not a pass/fail switch. It reads in several directions, and all but one of them are rejections:
— NOTHING on a hard crush: reject. Mountain laurel, sheep laurel, Lyonia, dog-hobble, swamp azalea, yaupon, inkberry, privet, Morella inodora.
— ALMOND, marzipan, maraschino: reject, and do not congratulate yourself on having found an aromatic leaf. Cherry laurel, hollyleaf cherry, Catalina cherry.
— ANISE or licorice: reject. Illicium.
— CAMPHOR, eucalyptus, a sharp medicinal punch: reject. California bay laurel.
— TURPENTINE or resinous-medicinal, especially on a leaf with rolled-under margins and rusty wool or white bloom beneath: reject. Labrador tea, bog laurel.
— SWEET BALSAM AND CANDLE WAX, on a leaf that is alternate, carries a field of sunken golden resin dots on a flat green underside, bleeds no white latex, has no raised glands on the petiole, has no vein running parallel just inside the margin, and grows on a multi-stemmed shrub: that is the only combination that goes in the pot.

Strength and handling. Northern bayberry is milder than Laurus nobilis, so use roughly twice as many leaves — two where a recipe calls for one. Wax myrtle is near enough to bay to swap one for one. Pacific wax myrtle is the least documented of the four in a kitchen; start with one leaf. Drying 10–14 days in a paper bag concentrates the aroma and takes off a grassy edge. Simmer at least 20–30 minutes to get anything out of a leaf; shorter than that and you have wasted it.

Never eat the leaf itself. Like a bay leaf it stays stiff and sharp-edged through any amount of cooking, and swallowed whole leaves of this kind have caused choking and tears to the throat and gut. Do not drink the leaves as a strong daily tea or take them as a concentrated extract; the aromatic resin is a flavouring dose, not a medicinal one, and concentrated bayberry preparations should be avoided in pregnancy. The gray waxy fruit is candle and soap stock, not food — essentially a wax shell on a stone, with no flesh on it. Leave the root bark entirely alone: it is a traditional emetic and astringent, strongly nauseating in quantity, and bayberry tannin from the bark has been reported as tumour-inducing in rodent feeding studies. Bayberry leaf itself needs no leaching or boiling to be made safe — but that is a statement about bayberry and about nothing else. It is not a statement about what else may be in your basket, and it is the sentence a reader is most likely to over-read. The safety of this dish rests entirely on what you put in, never on what you take out.

lookalikes.name: Cherry laurel — Carolina laurelcherry (Prunus caroliniana) and the planted and escaped English cherry laurel (Prunus laurocerasus)
lookalikes.tell: THIS IS THE ONE THAT KILLS PEOPLE LOOKING FOR A WILD BAY LEAF, AND IT DEFEATS THE SMELL TEST AS NORMALLY TAUGHT. A crushed cherry laurel leaf is strongly and pleasantly aromatic — marzipan, almond extract, maraschino — because bruising it releases hydrogen cyanide from cyanogenic glycosides. 'It smelled good when I crushed it' is therefore not an identification. You have to know the specific sweet balsam-and-candle-wax bayberry scent and reject anything almondy outright. Leaf tells that work on a picked green leaf in any month: cherry laurel leaves are thicker, glossier and darker, broadest near the apex, with a few sharp bristle-tipped teeth (older upper leaves often entire), and they carry extrafloral nectaries — two or more small raised dark glands on the petiole or on either side of the midrib near the leaf base. Bayberry has no nectaries at all; it has many small sunken resin dots scattered over the whole underside. Cherry laurel grows into a single-trunked tree to 30–40 ft with smooth gray bark; bayberry stays a multi-stemmed shrub. Snap a twig: cherry laurel wood smells of almond, bayberry of resin. The leaves run 1–2.5% cyanogenic glycosides, around 3.3 g prunasin equivalents per 100 g of fresh leaf, and WILTED OR DRIED LEAVES RELEASE MORE FREE CYANIDE THAN FRESH ONES — which is exactly what drying and simmering a 'bay leaf' does to it. AND THE DANGER DOES NOT LEAVE WITH THE LEAF. Prunasin and amygdalin are water-soluble: they come out of the leaf into the stock in the first few minutes of a simmer and stay there after you have fished the leaf out, to be cleaved to cyanide by your own gut flora. Distilled and infused 'laurel water' was a historical poison made from precisely this plant. If a cherry laurel leaf went into a pot, the pot is the poison — throw all of it out, including anything already served. Italy recorded 147 cherry laurel intoxications between 1995 and 2007 and 28 more in 2015, largely from confusion with culinary bay; 31 sheep in Scotland and 36 cattle in Ireland died on hedge clippings. P. caroliniana is native and common through the southeastern coastal plain from North Carolina to Texas and is planted everywhere as hedge and screen, routinely next to landscape wax myrtle; P. laurocerasus is a standard hedge shrub across the Northeast and is invasive in the Pacific Northwest, inside Pacific wax myrtle's range. Cyanide poisoning comes on fast — headache, dizziness, gasping, dilated pupils, weakness, convulsions, collapse. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) immediately; do not wait to see how it develops.

lookalikes.name: The California evergreen cherries and toyon — hollyleaf cherry (Prunus ilicifolia), Catalina cherry (P. lyonii) and toyon / Christmas berry (Heteromeles arbutifolia)
lookalikes.tell: THE WEST COAST'S CHERRY LAUREL, AND THIS ENTRY'S OWN CAVEAT POINTS STRAIGHT AT IT. 'A toothed leaf does not rule bayberry out' is true, and its cost is that it also means a toothed leaf does not rule these out. Hollyleaf cherry is the leathery, alternate, evergreen, spiny-toothed shrub of coastal California bluffs, canyon bottoms, dune scrub and chaparral — Morella californica's own ground as described in the habitat note above, from the Bay Area south into Baja. Catalina cherry is the island form with larger, mostly entire, flatter leaves, planted throughout coastal southern California and naturalised from those plantings; the two hybridise freely where both are grown, so margins on a garden plant tell you nothing. Toyon is the third leathery serrate evergreen on the same bluff and the same canyon, and it carries the same chemistry. Both cherries are Prunus: leaves and seeds hold prunasin and amygdalin and generate hydrogen cyanide as soon as the tissue is damaged, and WILTING AND DRYING RAISE THE FREE CYANIDE — exactly what you do to a leaf you intend to use as bay. Toyon's cyanogenic glycosides run through leaves and immature fruit, highest in new growth, and are enough to have killed horses off browse; the published levels are lower and less consistent than the cherries', which is a reason to reject it rather than a margin to work in. WHAT SEPARATES ALL THREE FROM PACIFIC WAX MYRTLE. (1) NO RESIN DOTS. Turn the leaf over against the light: the underside is a plain surface with nothing sunken in it, and a thumbnail finds nothing gritty. Morella californica has a field of sunken golden-orange glands, and on wax myrtle they are on both faces. (2) THE TEETH BITE. Hollyleaf cherry and toyon teeth are hard and spine-tipped and prick a finger drawn along the margin; hollyleaf cherry's blade is stiff, often cupped or wavy, and broadest at or below the middle. Wax myrtle's serrations are soft and flat and do not prick. (3) THE CRUSH. Prunus gives almond or nothing; toyon gives a bitter green nothing; wax myrtle gives sweet balsam and candle wax. Snap a twig — Prunus wood smells of bitter almond, and neither Morella nor Heteromeles does. (4) GLANDS. Both cherries carry small raised glands on the petiole or at the leaf base, which no Morella has. Fruit, in season, ends it: a single dark stone-fruit on the cherries and clusters of bright red pomes on toyon, never a bumpy gray wax ball. As with cherry laurel, the hazard survives the cook and stays in the broth after the leaf is out: if one of these went into a pot, discard the entire pot. Cyanide poisoning is fast — headache, dizziness, gasping, dilated pupils, weakness, convulsions, collapse. Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) immediately.

lookalikes.name: Oleander (Nerium oleander)
lookalikes.tell: Leaf arrangement settles this one in a single look, and it is worth making the look a habit: oleander leaves are OPPOSITE or in whorls of three, bayberry leaves are strictly alternate along the twig. Oleander's are long, narrow, stiff and leathery, uniformly dark green, perfectly entire, with a conspicuous pale midrib and fine parallel side veins running out to the edge; there are no resin dots and no scent on a hard crush. Break a leaf or a stem and it bleeds sticky white latex — bayberry never does, in any species or season. This matters because oleander is planted by the thousand along Gulf and South Atlantic coastal roads, parking lots, medians and old homesites, has escaped in the Deep South, and is among the commonest landscape shrubs in coastal California: the same disturbed coastal ground where wax myrtle is planted and volunteers, at the same height and habit. Every part carries cardiac glycosides (oleandrin, neriine) at a concentration where a single leaf is a plausible lethal dose for a child. THE COOKING-ADJACENT ROUTES ARE THE DOCUMENTED ONES, AND THEY ARE ALL BROTH ROUTES: deaths from leaves brewed as tea, from stems used as cooking skewers — where the wood was pulled out and the food still killed people — and from inhaling smoke off burning clippings. Oleandrin is heat-stable and water-soluble; taking the leaf out of the pot removes nothing. If oleander went into a pot, throw out everything in it and call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222). Nothing with milky sap and paired leaves goes in a stockpot, ever.

lookalikes.name: The grayanotoxin heaths of the same thickets — mountain laurel, sheep laurel and bog laurel (Kalmia latifolia, K. angustifolia, K. polifolia), swamp azalea (Rhododendron viscosum), fetterbush and staggerbush (Lyonia lucida, L. mariana, L. ferruginea) and dog-hobble (Leucothoe axillaris)
lookalikes.tell:
These are the leathery evergreen shrubs that physically grow interlaced with bayberry. NC State Extension puts Kalmia angustifolia in 'moist bogs, swamps, disturbed areas, roadsides, and dry pine forests' across the Northeast — northern bayberry ground, sand and peat alike — and rates its poison severity HIGH, as it does K. latifolia and Leucothoe axillaris; Lyonia lucida and Leucothoe build the southeastern pocosin and flatwoods thickets that wax myrtle rims, and bog laurel stands in the same saturated peat seam this entry sends you to at the sweet gale boundary.

DO NOT USE LEAF ARRANGEMENT ON THIS GROUP. Arrangement is the tell most often published for it and it clears nothing. NC State gives Kalmia latifolia as 'simple, alternate… occasionally opposite or whorled' and Leucothoe axillaris flatly as ALTERNATE, and every Lyonia is alternate. Only sheep laurel and bog laurel are reliably opposite or whorled. An alternate-leaved mountain laurel or dog-hobble passes an arrangement check cleanly, which would leave a beginner holding a deadly leaf with one test already 'passed'. This guide's sassafras entry deliberately separates this same group on texture and persistence instead of outline or arrangement, and so should you.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS, AND YOU NEED ALL THREE. (1) THE UNDERSIDE, held against the light. Morella carries a field of sunken golden to orange-brown resin dots in a flat green surface, gritty under a thumbnail. None of these heaths does: Kalmia latifolia is plain pale yellow-green beneath; K. polifolia is white-glaucous with margins rolled strongly under; Lyonia ferruginea is coated in rusty-brown peltate scales rather than clear golden dots; and Lyonia lucida — the closest match to bayberry at arm's length, being alternate, glossy, leathery, evergreen and on the same wet acid ground — carries a conspicuous vein running parallel to and just inside the leaf margin the entire way round, which no Morella has, with entire margins. (2) THE CRUSH. Thumbnail hard through the blade: these give you nothing at all, where bayberry gives sweet balsam and candle wax. (3) TEXTURE AND PERSISTENCE. These are thick, stiff, glossy, genuinely evergreen blades that bend or snap rather than tearing, on grey-brown woody twigs, and they are in full leaf in midwinter when northern bayberry is bare or down to a few tired semi-evergreen leaves.

All of them carry grayanotoxin (andromedotoxin), and it is concentrated in the LEAF, so a leaf simmered in a pot is the dangerous form. Grayanotoxins are non-volatile, HEAT-STABLE and water-soluble: they come out of the leaf into the liquid and stay in the broth after the leaf has been lifted out, exactly as they survive into heated mad honey and into dried laurel baled in hay. Salivation, vomiting, slowed heart, falling blood pressure, tingling, loss of coordination, seizures, paralysis, heart failure. This guide rates the grayanotoxin heaths deadly wherever they appear.

The working rule, and note which direction it runs: IF A LEATHERY LEAF GIVES YOU NOTHING ON THE CRUSH, PUT IT DOWN, whatever else it looks like. That is a rejection rule only. It does not run backwards. An aromatic leathery leaf is not thereby safe — cherry laurel, Illicium and the Labrador teas below all smell wonderful.

lookalikes.name: The Labrador teas — bog Labrador tea (Rhododendron groenlandicum, syn. Ledum groenlandicum) and western or trapper's tea (R. columbianum, syn. R. neoglandulosum, Ledum glandulosum)
lookalikes.tell:
THE PLANT THAT DEFEATS THE POSITIVE AROMA RULE THE WAY CHERRY LAUREL DEFEATS THE NEGATIVE ONE, and it stands in the exact seam this entry sends you to three separate times — where a dune swale or pond edge grades into saturated peat in the Northeast and around the Great Lakes, and in the Pacific Northwest bogs and montane wet meadows where Morella californica's range overlaps Myrica gale's. These are ALTERNATE, leathery, entire, evergreen heaths, 1–5 ft, and they are strongly and pleasantly aromatic on a crush — resinous, camphoraceous, turpentine-and-tea — so a reader who has learned 'no smell means put it down' will read the smell as confirmation. It is not confirmation of anything.

THE UNDERSIDE SETTLES IT IN ONE LOOK, and it is a look you should be taking on every leaf anyway. R. groenlandicum has margins ROLLED STRONGLY UNDER and the whole lower surface felted in dense RUSTY-ORANGE WOOL you can rub into a visible fuzz with a thumb — a continuous mat of hair, not discrete sunken dots in a green surface. R. columbianum is less woolly but its underside carries scattered stalked glands and fine hairs, and the margins still roll. A Morella underside is a flat green surface with glandular pits sunk into it; rub it and nothing comes off. The leaves are also narrower and more strap-like, 1–2.5 in, and borne in crowded clusters at the shoot tips rather than spaced evenly along the twig, and the fruit is a small dry five-parted capsule that splits from the base — never a gray wax ball.

WHY IT IS GRADED WITH THE GRAYANOTOXIN HEATHS. R. columbianum carries GRAYANOTOXIN and is the poisonous one of the pair; both carry the terpenoid ledol, and the standard caution on the genus is that the tea must not be steeped long or drunk daily. The ethnobotanical use of R. groenlandicum as a short-steeped beverage is real, but it is not licence here: the two species are not reliably separable by a beginner, a 20–30 minute stock simmer is nothing like a short steep, and bog laurel (Kalmia polifolia), squarely deadly, stands in the same peat with similarly narrow rolled-margin leaves that are WHITE-glaucous rather than rusty beneath. Aromatic is not a pass. Aromatic in one specific way — sweet balsam and candle wax, on a leaf with a flat green underside full of sunken golden dots and no fuzz at all — is a pass.

lookalikes.name: Florida anise and yellow anise / swamp star anise (Illicium floridanum, I. parviflorum)
lookalikes.tell:
THE SOUTHEAST'S AROMATIC-CRUSH-POSITIVE HAZARD, and it occupies both of this entry's highest-risk situations at once. In the wild it holds streamhead bogs, bayheads, ravine bottoms, seepage slopes and bay-forest rims across the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and Georgia — the identical ground this entry assigns to Morella inodora and to the wax myrtle pocosin rim. In the landscape it is one of the most heavily planted evergreen shrubs in the Southeast, standing in clipped hedges and foundation beds shoulder to shoulder with landscape wax myrtle, which is the exact hedgerow exposure this entry flags as its main practical risk. At a glance the leaves read as bayberry: ALTERNATE (though crowded into a pseudo-whorl at the shoot tip), simple, thick, leathery, glossy dark green above and paler below, 2–6 in, on a multi-stemmed shrub, and STRONGLY AROMATIC when bruised — anise, licorice, or what NC State's toolbox calls a gin-and-tonic smell; I. floridanum's is sharper and some people read it as fishy.

THREE TELLS. (1) SCENT IDENTITY, which is the whole reason the crush test has to be run for a specific smell rather than for 'aromatic'. Anise and licorice are not sweet balsam and candle wax. The moment you get anise, you stop. (2) NO RESIN DOTS. The aroma comes from oil distributed through the tissue, not from glands; the underside is a plain pale surface with nothing sunken in it and nothing gritty under a thumbnail. (3) MARGINS ENTIRE and often distinctly wavy, on a reddish-purple leaf stalk in I. floridanum, with the leaves crowded in rosettes at the branch ends rather than spread along the twig. The fruit is a flat many-pointed star, which nothing else here produces.

CHEMISTRY, STATED HONESTLY. The genus makes sesquiterpene lactones — anisatin, neoanisatin, pseudoanisatin — which are potent non-competitive GABA antagonists, and the Japanese star anise (I. anisatum) cases are the reference point: seven infants at one Florida hospital with seizures, jitteriness, vomiting, nystagmus and myoclonus after home-brewed star anise tea, which is why star anise infusions are not given to infants. Reported anisatin content in the two American species is lower and genuinely disputed in the literature, and NC State rates both I. floridanum and I. parviflorum poison severity LOW while still listing leaves, fruit and seeds as poisonous to humans and livestock. Treat the dispute as a reason to keep it out of the pot, not as a margin to work in: the toxin is heat-stable and water-extracted, every documented human case is an infusion, and a 20–30 minute simmer is an infusion.

lookalikes.name: Groundsel tree / eastern baccharis (Baccharis halimifolia)
lookalikes.tell: Shares exactly the same dune edges, marsh borders, fencerows and old fields at exactly the same height, and in the Southeast the two routinely grow into each other. The tell usually published for it — 'in autumn it is covered in conspicuous fluffy white seed heads' — is no use for most of the leaf-picking year and only ever works on female plants, so do not build your check on it. What works year-round, on leaf and twig: Baccharis leaves are thick, gray-green and obovate with only one to five large, coarse, sharp teeth per side on the upper half; each leaf shows three prominent veins arising at or near the base (the composite-family trait), where bayberry has one midrib with pinnate side veins; and the underside carries no dense field of golden resin dots. Its twigs are green and distinctly angled or ridged, while bayberry twigs are round, gray-brown and gland-dotted, and smell resinous when scratched. Do not lean on the claim that 'Baccharis has no smell' either — it is itself a resinous plant, and a crushed leaf can smell faintly of turpentine or of very little depending on season and individual. The honest statement is that it never smells of sweet balsam and candle wax. Leaves and flowers contain cardioactive glycosides; cattle and sheep have been killed eating it, and Alabama Extension handles it as a poisonous weed.

lookalikes.name: Sweet gale / bog myrtle (Myrica gale)
lookalikes.tell: The lookalike that passes every aroma test, because it genuinely is an aromatic, resin-dotted member of this family — it is used as a seasoning and beer-bittering herb in northern Europe, which is exactly why foragers assume it is interchangeable. It is not. Its essential oil is toxic in quantity, the seed oil should never be ingested, and the plant is a listed abortifacient, contraindicated in pregnancy. Separate it by ground and by fruit, never by smell. Sweet gale stands in saturated peat at the edges of bog and fen pools, lake shores and slow streams, frequently with its feet in standing water; bayberry sits on sand that drains. Sweet gale is smaller, 2–5 ft, its leaves are strongly wedge-shaped and widest right up near the tip with a few coarse teeth confined to the very end of the leaf, and its fruit is a short brown cone-like burr of winged nutlets — never the round gray wax-coated ball of a bayberry. The overlap is real, not theoretical: it runs across the northern tier into New England, New York and the Great Lakes and down the Pacific coast into Washington and Oregon, so it meets northern bayberry wherever a dune swale grades into peat, and meets Pacific wax myrtle in the Northwest. Note that this is the same peat seam that holds bog laurel and the Labrador teas, so 'I have found the aromatic bog shrub' resolves to at least three different plants, two of them graded deadly here.

lookalikes.name: Yaupon and inkberry holly (Ilex vomitoria, I. glabra) and naturalised privet (Ligustrum sinense, L. japonicum)
lookalikes.tell: The other small-leaved leathery evergreens of southeastern thickets, hedgerows and dune scrub, and by sheer abundance the most likely wrong leaf to end up in your hand. Neither has resin dots and neither gives you anything on a hard crush — that alone decides it. Beyond that: privet is opposite-leaved with small blunt entire leaves; yaupon is alternate but its leaves are only 0.5–1.5 in, rounded at the tip, with even rounded crenate teeth right around the margin, on stiff whitish-gray twigs held at wide angles; inkberry's are longer with a few teeth near the tip only. Fruit settles it too — shiny red (yaupon), black (inkberry, privet), never the bumpy gray-white wax ball. Holly berries cause vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain, and privet berries and foliage are rated toxic to people and livestock. Yaupon leaves do make a legitimate caffeinated tea, the one native North American caffeine plant, but they are not a bay leaf and will contribute nothing to a pot except tannin.

lookalikes.name: Odorless bayberry (Morella inodora)
lookalikes.tell: Same genus, same gray waxy fruit, same wetlands — and no scent whatsoever, which is the entire point of listing it. It grows in acid streamhead bogs, bayheads, pond edges and stream banks along the northern Gulf: the Florida panhandle, southernmost Alabama and Mississippi, eastern Louisiana and southwestern Georgia — which is also Illicium ground, so this is a place where a scentless Morella and a strongly anise-scented non-Morella stand in the same bay swamp. Its leaves are thicker and larger than wax myrtle's, to 5 in, glossy, ovate to elliptic and entire, and crushing one gives you nothing at all. It will not hurt you, but it is the reason the aroma check has to be run POSITIVELY on every leaf you pick: you confirm a bayberry by smelling the bayberry smell on that particular leaf, not by reasoning that the shrub is a Morella and therefore fine. It is also uncommon and of conservation concern across parts of its small range — leave it standing.

lookalikes.name: California bay laurel / pepperwood (Umbellularia californica)
lookalikes.tell: A West Coast problem only, and not a poisoning risk — but it shares Pacific wax myrtle's coastal canyons and bluff slopes, it is powerfully aromatic, and it gets picked by mistake and then used in bayberry quantities. It is a tree, to 80 ft, with much larger leaves (2–5 in), smooth-margined and willow-like, no resin dots, and a sharp camphor-and-eucalyptus punch nothing like bayberry's sweet resin — which is why the crush test has to reject camphor as firmly as it rejects almond and anise. It is safe to cook with in small amounts and is in fact the far stronger seasoning — one leaf where you would use four of bayberry — but a bayberry-sized dose turns a dish bitter and medicinal, and deeply inhaling a freshly crushed leaf gives some people an immediate violent headache, which is where the name 'headache tree' came from.

entry.harvest:
PICK ONE LEAF AT A TIME, and look at each one as it comes off. Never run a closed hand down a stem and never strip a branch into a bag — that is how a laurel, cherry, Illicium or Labrador tea leaf arrives without anyone having decided to pick it, and once leaves are dried and mixed together the evidence of what went in is gone while every hazard here is still fully potent. Spread the picking in a single layer and check every leaf again before it goes into a jar. Take a few leaves from many shrubs rather than stripping one stem, and pick from the outside of the thicket. Strip-picking costs more here than it looks: these are slow-growing dune and pocosin stabilisers that hold sand and peat in place, and on a northeastern back dune a bayberry thicket is often the only woody cover there is.

PICK THE NORTHEAST IN LEAF — ROUGHLY JUNE THROUGH SEPTEMBER. Wax myrtle and Pacific wax myrtle are genuinely evergreen and can be picked year-round, but from about November to April northern bayberry is bare or down to a few tired semi-evergreen leaves, while every dangerous plant on this list — cherry laurel, mountain laurel, dog-hobble, Lyonia, bog laurel, Labrador tea, Illicium, hollyleaf cherry — is in full glossy leaf. A leathery evergreen leaf taken off a northeastern dune thicket in January is more likely to be one of them than bayberry, and the shrub you are standing at cannot vouch for the leaf in your hand.

Leave the fruit entirely, whatever you are doing with the leaves. The gray wax drupes are one of the very few winter fat sources on the northeastern coast that a bird can actually digest — the yellow-rumped warbler is among the only vertebrates able to break down the wax, which is what lets it winter further north than any other warbler, and tree swallows staging on the coast in autumn lean on the same fruit; it hangs on the shrub until April. Ignore the standard advice to 'take leaves from the male plants': they are dioecious, but you cannot reliably sex one outside flower or fruit, and a handful of leaves costs a female shrub very little. Just leave the berries alone.

Check the rules before you pick, because this species grows disproportionately on protected ground. Collecting plants or plant parts is prohibited in National Park Service units under 36 CFR 2.1 — which takes in Cape Cod, Assateague, Cape Hatteras, Cape Lookout, Canaveral, Gulf Islands and Padre Island national seashores — and requires a permit on most National Wildlife Refuges. Separately, dune vegetation is legally protected in its own right in most Atlantic coastal states and in many beach towns: stay off the primary dune, and stay out of fenced dune-restoration plots and shorebird nesting areas entirely, whatever the foraging rules happen to say.

Two practical hazards inside the thicket. Poison ivy grows as a shrub through northeastern bayberry stands and climbs up through them, and poison oak does the same on the West Coast — you will be reaching blind into exactly the height band they occupy, so look before you put a hand in, and never crush a doubtful leaf to smell it until you have looked at it. And these thickets carry a heavy tick load right through the harvest season.

Finally, do not pick from roadside verges, medians or clipped landscape hedges. That is where most of the accessible wax myrtle in the Southeast actually is, it is routinely sprayed, and it is precisely where it stands shoulder to shoulder with oleander, cherry laurel and Florida anise — three of the plants that can put you in hospital, all of them planted for the same reasons and often in the same row.

blocking: The single 'pass' combination in `parts` is satisfied by a plant this entry itself grades toxic. The rule reads: sweet balsam and candle wax, alternate, sunken golden resin dots on a flat green underside, no latex, no petiole glands, no intramarginal vein, multi-stemmed shrub — 'that is the only combination that goes in the pot.' Myrica gale passes every clause of that: it is alternate, genuinely resin-dotted (same family), aromatic, latex-free, gland-free, vein-free and multi-stemmed. The entry separates sweet gale correctly in its lookalike tell (by ground and by fruit, never by smell) but never carries those disqualifiers back into the decision rule a reader will actually run. Since sweet gale is a listed abortifacient contraindicated in pregnancy, the gap has a real consequence. Fix is one clause: add to the pass line 'on ground that drains rather than saturated peat or standing water, with teeth not confined to the very tip of the leaf, and bearing round gray wax berries rather than a brown cone-like burr.'

months is [0..11] while regions includes 'northeast', and forageFor() in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/data/foraging.ts filters strictly on region x month — so /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/components/ForageSection.tsx will list this under 'Coast & salt marsh' for a Northeast user in January and count it in 'N to look for in January'. That is precisely the window the entry's own harvest text calls the most dangerous: 'A leathery evergreen leaf taken off a northeastern dune thicket in January is more likely to be one of them than bayberry.' The warning exists only in `harvest`, which renders under 'Leave enough' after five paragraphs of `parts`; neither the collapsed row nor `habitat` nor `parts` carries any seasonal cue, so a partial reader gets a green light for the one scenario where the target plant is absent and every deadly lookalike is in full glossy leaf. The union-of-regions months convention used elsewhere in the corpus (e.g. Golden Chanterelle's winter months) is harmless there because an out-of-season listing just yields nothing; here it schedules the failure. Fix either way: trim months to the northern in-leaf window (roughly [4,5,6,7,8,9]) and state the southern/Pacific year-round availability in prose, or lead `habitat` with the June–September Northeast sentence so it appears in the collapsed row's lead and cannot be skipped.
